title.text: Can I trust this model? Overfitting, cross-validation and leakage

objects.text: How do we know a model that predicts crusher energy demand will still work on a crusher it has never seen?

CML3113  |  Mining and Petroleum Engineering  |  Week 10, class 3 of 4  |  Friday 20 November 2026, 08:00 to 11:00
KLAi  |  International University of East Africa  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. In the first two classes you built models that predict crusher energy demand and models that answer yes or no. Today we ask the question an engineer must always ask: can I trust this?

A score that looks good is not enough. We learn how a model fools us, and how to test it so that it cannot.

title.text: Today in one view: what you will leave with

objects.text: By the end of today you can
Explain underfitting, a good fit and overfitting (the bias-variance trade-off), and tune the hyperparameter max_depth with a validation curve
Work out training error, validation error, the generalisation gap, and a cross-validation mean and standard deviation, by hand
Score a model with K-fold and GroupKFold cross-validation, and report the mean with its standard deviation
Name three kinds of data leakage and use a checklist that blocks them

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can explain underfitting, a good fit and overfitting, the bias-variance trade-off, and you can tune max_depth, a hyperparameter, by looking at a validation curve. You can work out the training error, the validation error, the generalisation gap, and the mean and standard deviation of cross-validation scores, by hand.

You can score a model with K-fold and GroupKFold. And you can name three kinds of data leakage and keep a checklist that blocks them. Nothing is submitted today. At the end I explain the project, which opens online on Monday 23 November, and how this class counts.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent?
2.  In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)?
3.  What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3?

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Class 2. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent? Take a moment.

A good answer: It finds none of the real positive cases, so its recall is 0. Accuracy hides that.

Question two. In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)? Say it to yourself first.

What I hope you said: False negative: the model said no (negative) and the truth was yes (positive). False positive: the model said yes and the truth was no.

Question three. What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3? Write a word or two down.

The short answer: Recall stayed at 1.00. False positives went from 1 to 2.

Keep these three in mind, because today builds on them.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Class 2

rows.text: Why is a majority-class baseline (a model that always predicts no) a poor model, even when its accuracy is about 80 percent?
It finds none of the real positive cases, so its recall is 0. Accuracy hides that.
In a confusion matrix, what is a false negative (FN) and what is a false positive (FP)?
False negative: the model said no (negative) and the truth was yes (positive). False positive: the model said yes and the truth was no.
What happened to recall and false positives when we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3?
Recall stayed at 1.00. False positives went from 1 to 2.

slides.notes:
Here are the answers, so you can check yourself and use this slide to revise. A majority-class baseline, a model that always predicts no, can have a high accuracy, but it finds no real positive case, so its recall is zero. A false negative is a no when the truth was yes, and a false positive is a yes when the truth was no.

When we lowered the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 on the validation rows: Recall stayed at 1.00. False positives went from 1 to 2. Today we ask a different question about the same models: can we trust a score at all?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: The model fits the noise in the training set (it nearly memorises it) and does worse on new rows. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to learn the pattern.
Scoring a model K times. The rows are cut into K parts called folds. Each fold takes one turn as the validation fold (held-out fold).
Information the model would not have at prediction time (held-out rows, or the target itself) reaches it while it is trained, so the score looks better than it really is.
Too simple a model misses the pattern (high bias, underfitting). Too flexible a model chases noise (high variance, overfitting).
A fixed number (random_state in scikit-learn) that makes a random choice repeat exactly.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. Overfitting is when a model fits the noise in its training set and does worse on new rows. Underfitting is the opposite: too simple to learn the pattern. Cross-validation means scoring a model K times. The rows are cut into K parts called folds, and each fold takes one turn as the validation fold, which some books call the held-out fold.

Data leakage is information the model would not have at prediction time, such as held-out rows or the target itself, reaching it while it is trained, so the score looks better than it is. The bias-variance trade-off is the industry name for the balance between too simple and too flexible.

And a random seed, set with random_state, makes a random choice repeat exactly. We use all five before the end.

title.text:
A model that looks good on paper
can fail on a new machine or site

objects.text: A model is built from data on four crushers and then used on a fifth crusher.
The power plan for the new pit is chosen from the model’s prediction.
If the prediction is wrong, the energy bill holds a surprise.

slides.notes:
Start with a story from your own field. A model is built from data on four crushers and then used on a fifth crusher. The power plan for the new pit is chosen from the model’s prediction. If the prediction is wrong, the energy bill holds a surprise.

In the office the model looked excellent, so everybody trusted it. The trouble is that the office score came from rows the model had already been trained on, or from a test that was too easy. Today is about checking a model the way real life will check it.

Have you ever trusted a number from a machine or a spreadsheet and then been surprised?

title.text: A model must do well on rows it has never seen

objects.alt: A model must do well on rows it has never seen

objects.text: Generalisation means doing well on held-out data: rows the model has never seen.

runs.text: The tree was trained on the training set, so its error there is almost zero.
The validation set was held out. On it the prediction error is far larger. The difference is the generalisation gap.

slides.notes:
Here is one tree, grown ten questions deep, scored two ways. The training set is the rows it was trained on, and there its error is 0.00 kWh/t, which is almost perfect. The validation set was held out, and there its error is 1.18 kWh/t. The difference between the two is called the generalisation gap.

Doing well on held-out rows it has never seen is called generalisation, and it is the only thing we really want. A score on rows the model was trained on tells us about its memory, and a score on new rows tells us about its skill. Which score would you show a client?

title.text:
Underfitting, a good fit and
overfitting look like three students

objects.alt: Underfitting, a good fit and overfitting look like three students

objects.text: The marks in the picture are illustrative (made up). Each student stands for one kind of model.

runs.text: Practice paper = training set. New paper = held-out rows.
Bias-variance trade-off: too simple a model misses the pattern, too flexible a model chases noise.

slides.notes:
Think of three students. The first read nothing, so the practice paper and the new paper both go badly. That is underfitting: a model too simple to learn the pattern, which the industry calls high bias. The second understood the ideas, so the marks are good on both papers.

That is a good fit. The third memorised last year’s answers. Perfect on the practice paper and poor on the new paper. That is overfitting: the model fits the noise, which the industry calls high variance. Balancing the two is the bias-variance trade-off. The practice paper stands for the training set, the new paper for held-out rows, and the marks are made up.

Can you think of someone who passed by memory and then struggled on the job?

title.text:
The validation curve: as max_depth grows, training
error keeps falling but validation error stops improving

objects.alt: The validation curve: as max_depth grows, training error keeps falling but validation error stops improving

objects.text: A validation curve plots both errors against max_depth, a hyperparameter (set before training).

runs.text: Each dot is one tree. Black: training error. Red: validation error. Between them: the gap.
Depths 1 and 2: both errors high. From depth 7: training error near 0. Gold: chosen depth 5.

slides.notes:
This is a validation curve from our data. Each point is a tree with a different max_depth, a hyperparameter: a setting we choose before training. The black line is the training error, and it falls all the way to 0.00. At depths 1 and 2 both errors are high: that is underfitting.

From depth 7 up, the training error is near 0: those trees fit the training rows almost exactly, which is overfitting. The red line is the validation error. After depth 5 the validation error rises a little, to 1.26 kWh/t at depth 8. The gold band is the depth we choose, depth 5; the next slides show why.

In Class 1 you tried depths 1, 2 and 8: this is what you were seeing. Where does the gap start to grow?

title.text:
Training error, validation error and the
generalisation gap are short formulas

objects.alt: Training error, validation error and the generalisation gap are short formulas

rows.text: Mean absolute error: the average size of the prediction error. The small label train or val says which rows
How many rows. The small label tr means training and va means validation
A row number. The sum adds up the rows of that group
The real target of row i, and the model’s prediction for it. The bars | | drop any minus sign
crusher energy demand and the tree’s answer, in kWh/t

slides.notes:
Class 1 gave you the MAE. Here it is again, written for two groups of rows. The training error adds up the size of the prediction error on every training row, then divides by the number of training rows. The validation error does the same on the validation rows.

The bars mean the size of the error, so a plus or a minus makes no difference. In our data at depth 10 the training error is 0.00 kWh/t and the validation error is 1.18 kWh/t. Which rows is the tree trained on, and which rows does it never see?

title.text:
The generalisation gap is the validation
error minus the training error

objects.alt: The generalisation gap is the validation error minus the training error

rows.text: Generalisation gap: how much worse the model is on new rows
Validation error, from the formula before
Training error, from the formula before

objects.text: Small gap: similar error on new rows. Big gap: overfitting. We choose max_depth by validation error.

slides.notes:
The generalisation gap is one subtraction: the validation error minus the training error. At depth 10 it is 1.18 minus 0.00, which is 1.18 kWh/t. At our chosen depth, depth 5, it is 1.12 minus 0.33, which is 0.79 kWh/t. A small gap says the model does about as well on new rows as on its training set.

A big gap says it is overfitting, fitting the noise in the training set. At depth 5 the gap is smaller than at depth 10, yet the training error is already below the validation error. We choose by the validation error alone. Next, five depths in one table.

title.text:
Five depths in one table: leaf nodes,
errors and the generalisation gap

objects.text: MAE in kWh/t. A leaf node is a final node: it holds the prediction. The Class 1 linear regression model scores 0.67 kWh/t, better than every tree: the target is close to a straight line, and a tree only makes steps.

slides.notes:
Same numbers as the curve, in a table. Look at the leaf nodes, the final nodes at the bottom of the tree. Every row ends in exactly one leaf node, and the tree gives every row in it the same prediction. At depth 1 there are 2 leaf nodes.

At depth 10 there are 58, for only 58 training rows, so the tree is close to keeping one answer for each row. That is overfitting. The last column is the generalisation gap from the last slide. One more fact for later: the linear regression model from Class 1 scored 0.67 kWh/t, better than every tree.

Why?

The target rises smoothly, close to a straight line, and a tree can only make steps. So today the tree is our test case for trust. Which depth would you call too deep?

title.text:
We choose max_depth on the validation
set and keep the test set sealed

objects.alt: We choose max_depth on the validation set and keep the test set sealed

objects.text: Each set is made of whole equipment groups. The picture shows the rows in each set.

runs.text: Only 15 validation rows, so a score can move by luck. Never tune on the test set.
Test set rule: open it once, after the model and any threshold are chosen. Refit the chosen model on E1 to E5, score it once on E6.

slides.notes:
How did we choose depth 5?

We looked at the validation set only. The picture shows the three sets: training from groups E1 to E4, validation from group E5, and test from group E6. The test set has one rule. It is opened once, at the very end, after the model and any decision threshold are chosen.

For that final number the chosen model is refitted on all development rows, E1 to E5, and scored once on E6. In the project a supplied cell opens the test set once for you, and Class 4 shows the step in full. The validation set has only 15 rows, so its scores are noisy.

We need a rule that does not chase small differences. Why would the lowest score alone be risky?

title.text:
Tuning a hyperparameter: choose the simplest
max_depth within 5 percent of the lowest validation error

objects.alt: Tuning a hyperparameter: choose the simplest max_depth within 5 percent of the lowest validation error

rows.text: Validation MAE of the tree with max_depth d
The lowest validation MAE over depths 1 to 10
The tolerance limit: the lowest value plus 5 percent
The chosen depth: the smallest d that passes

objects.text: Depth 3 (1.175) misses the limit (1.174) by a hair: the rule is sensitive. d* = chosen max_depth (parsimony).

slides.notes:
Choosing a hyperparameter such as max_depth is called tuning a hyperparameter. Our rule: find the lowest validation error, V min. For us it is 1.118 kWh/t, at depth 5. Multiply by 1.05 to get the limit, 1.174 kWh/t. Any depth at or below the limit passes: 5, 6.

We take the smallest, depth 5, because a simpler tree is easier to explain. That is parsimony. Depth 3 (1.175) misses the limit (1.174) by a hair: the rule is sensitive. The 5 percent is our own choice and it is not a law. The chosen depth can also move with the random seed, as we see later.

What would change if we multiplied by 1.00 instead of 1.05?

title.text:
One split can be lucky, so K-fold cross-validation
lets every fold take a turn as the validation fold

objects.alt: One split can be lucky, so K-fold cross-validation lets every fold take a turn as the validation fold

objects.text: K-fold cross-validation cuts the 58 training rows into K = 5 folds (parts of the rows), in the order the rows appear (no shuffle).

runs.text: In each line, the tree is trained on 4 folds and scored on the gold validation fold.
Rows of E1 to E4 are interleaved: every fold holds all four groups (fold 1: E1 4, E2 4, E3 2, E4 2).

slides.notes:
A single validation split is one test on one day, and the day may be lucky or unlucky. K-fold cross-validation takes several tests. Cut the 58 training rows into five folds. In the first line of the picture, the tree is trained on folds two to five, and fold one is the validation fold, also called the held-out fold.

Some books call it the test fold, but it is not the sealed test set E6. Here are the five scores for a depth-4 tree, from 0.87 to 1.47 kWh/t. One warning: the rows of the four groups are interleaved, so every fold holds rows of all four crushers.

The model has already met each crusher in training. Is that how it will be used on a new crusher?

title.text:
K-fold gives k scores, and we report
their mean and their standard deviation

objects.alt: K-fold gives k scores, and we report their mean and their standard deviation

rows.text: The MAE when fold j is the validation fold (j is the fold number)
The number of folds, so the number of scores
The mean (average) of the k scores (s with a bar)
Sample standard deviation: typical distance of a score from the mean. np.std(scores, ddof=1)

slides.notes:
Two formulas turn the five scores into two numbers. The mean adds up the k scores and divides by k. The standard deviation asks how far each score sits from the average, squares those distances so plus and minus cannot cancel, adds them, divides by k minus 1, and takes the square root.

Dividing by k minus 1 gives the sample standard deviation, the usual choice for a few scores. In NumPy you write ddof equals 1, because np.std divides by k unless you say so. Our five scores give a mean of 1.16 kWh/t and a standard deviation of 0.26 kWh/t.

A small standard deviation means the folds agree. A large one means the score depends on which fold you ask. Next we work it by hand on our five scores.

title.text:
By hand: our five fold scores give
their mean and standard deviation

objects.text: Mean = 5.82 / 5 = 1.16 kWh/t. Sum of squares / (k - 1) = 0.276 / 4 = 0.069. Square root = 0.26 kWh/t, the standard deviation. Worked from unrounded scores, so the last digit can differ.

slides.notes:
Let us work it by hand on the five real scores from our depth-4 tree. The scores add up to 5.82, so the mean is 1.16 kWh/t. Each score has a distance from that mean, some above and some below, and the distances add up to zero. We square them, and the squares add up to 0.276.

Divide by k minus 1, which is four, to get 0.069, and the square root of that is 0.26 kWh/t. That is the standard deviation you will see in the notebook. Compare it with the mean. Is it small or large?

title.text:
GroupKFold holds out a whole equipment group
in each fold, which is how the model is really used

objects.alt: GroupKFold holds out a whole equipment group in each fold, which is how the model is really used

objects.text: GroupKFold keeps each group whole: each of E1 to E4 is held out once (scikit-learn picks the order).

runs.text: Plain K-fold put every crusher in every fold. Here the tree trains on three groups and is scored on the fourth, like a new site.
Score s_g: MAE on group g. Mean and sample standard deviation as before (divide by 3).

slides.notes:
Plain K-fold mixes rows from every group, so the model has already seen the same crusher while it is trained. In real use a new crusher arrives, and nobody has seen it. GroupKFold fixes that by keeping each equipment group whole. In each fold it holds out one group, trains on the other three, and scores the held-out group.

Each of E1 to E4 takes one turn, in an order scikit-learn chooses to balance the fold sizes. The four scores run from 0.84 to 1.20 kWh/t, with a mean of 1.09 and a sample standard deviation of 0.17, the same two formulas with four scores. Class 4 shows a five-group version.

Which design looks more like your work?

title.text:
The same max_depth 4 tree gets three
different scores, depending on how we test it

rows.text: K-fold, k = 5 (rows in order, no shuffle)

objects.text: MAE in kWh/t. The single E5 score is within about one standard deviation of both means: the normal spread from one fold to another. The standard deviation shows how far to trust each mean.

slides.notes:
Here is the same tree scored three ways. The single split on group E5 says 1.20. Plain K-fold says 1.16, with a standard deviation of 0.26. GroupKFold says 1.09, with a standard deviation of 0.17. The single E5 score is within about one standard deviation of both means: the normal spread from one fold to another.

One split could just as easily have been luckier or unluckier. Report the mean and the standard deviation, and say how the folds were made. Which of the three would you quote to a client, and what would you add?

title.text:
Data leakage is information the model would not
have at prediction time reaching it during training

objects.alt: Data leakage is information the model would not have at prediction time reaching it during training

objects.text: Data leakage: information the model would not have at prediction time (held-out rows, or the target itself) reaches it while it is trained.

runs.text: Held-out rows are the validation or test rows. The dashed red arrow is the leakage.
The score looks excellent, then the model fails on real new rows.

slides.notes:
Now the second big danger. Data leakage means information the model would not have at prediction time, such as held-out rows or the target itself, reaches it while it is trained. The picture shows the normal path along the bottom: the training rows train the model, and then the model gets a score.

The held-out rows are the validation or test rows, and they must stay out of training. If anything from them slips in, along the red arrow, the model has seen the answers. The score then looks excellent, and the model fails on the first real new rows. The worst part is that nothing warns you.

There is no error message, only a score that is too good. Have you seen a result that looked too good to be true?

title.text: Data leakage comes in three common kinds

objects.alt: Data leakage comes in three common kinds

objects.text: All three make the score look too good.

slides.notes:
Three kinds cover most cases. Train-test contamination: validation rows end up in the training set, for example by joining two files, or by tuning on the test rows again and again. Preprocessing leakage: an imputer, which fills missing values, or a scaler, which rescales columns to a common scale, is fitted on all rows before the split, so the training set carries information about the validation rows.

Target leakage: a feature is computed from the target, such as a column that is only filled in after the failure has happened. We show each one with real numbers.

title.text:
Train-test contamination: validation rows in
the training set make the score look perfect

objects.alt: Train-test contamination: validation rows in the training set make the score look perfect

objects.text: Same max_depth 10 tree. Only the training set changed.

runs.text: In the leaky run the tree was already trained on the validation rows, so it reproduces their answers: it has already seen them.
The honest score is the real one.

slides.notes:
This is the real demonstration from our data. The same tree, depth ten. In the honest version the validation rows are held out, and the validation error is 1.18 kWh/t. In the leaky version we put the validation rows into the training set first, which is train-test contamination.

The error drops to 0.01. The tree has simply memorised those rows, so the leaky score is almost perfect and tells us nothing. Nobody would do this on purpose, but a join or a copy and paste can do it quietly. Which of the two scores would predict a new machine?

title.text:
A Pipeline fits the imputer on the training set
only, which prevents preprocessing leakage

objects.alt: A Pipeline fits the imputer on the training set only, which prevents preprocessing leakage

objects.text: Median of ambient_c: 26.07 from the training set, 25.37 from training plus validation rows (73 rows, leakage). Only one value is missing, so the score did not change.

slides.notes:
Preprocessing leakage is the quiet one. If you fill missing values, or scale columns, using all the rows, the validation rows have helped to decide the fill. In our data the median ambient temperature is 26.07 from the training set and 25.37 from the training and validation rows together.

We tried both, and the validation error did not change, because only one value is missing. So here the habit costs nothing. That is exactly why it is dangerous: a clean score does not prove a clean method. The fix is a Pipeline, which chains the imputer and the tree.

In every fold it fits the imputer on the training folds only, then fills the validation fold with those same numbers.

title.text:
The pipeline rule: fit on the training
set only, then apply the same numbers

objects.alt: The pipeline rule: fit on the training set only, then apply the same numbers

rows.text: Row i, column j, the value x_ij there, n_tr training rows. In preprocessing leakage, i also runs over validation rows
Median of column j over the training rows
Mean and standard deviation of column j, training rows (divide by n_tr, Class 2)
The z-score (standardised value) of row i in column j

slides.notes:
Here is the pipeline rule as a formula. The median for column j is taken over the training rows only. The mean and the standard deviation for column j are also taken over the training rows only. Then the same three numbers are applied to every row, including the validation rows.

The leakage is simple to state: if the row number i also runs over the validation rows, the imputer or scaler has seen them. Take row one of our training data. Its load is 59.15. Subtract the mean 59.89, divide by the standard deviation 22.73, and the z-score is -0.03.

Class 2 used this scaler, and the pipeline does it for you inside every fold.

title.text:
Target leakage: a feature built from the target
gives a great score that cannot be repeated

objects.alt: Target leakage: a feature built from the target gives a great score that cannot be repeated

objects.text: With that feature a max_depth 4 tree scores 0.31 kWh/t. With honest features it scores 1.20 kWh/t.

runs.text: target_rounded is the target rounded to a whole number. At prediction time the target is unknown.
A feature recorded after the event is also target leakage.

slides.notes:
This is target leakage. Suppose someone adds a feature that is the target rounded to a whole number. A depth-4 tree with that feature scores 0.31 kWh/t on the validation rows, against 1.20 without it. It looks like a miracle. But when a new reading arrives, the target is exactly what we do not know yet, so the feature cannot be filled in.

Real examples are a repair code written after the failure, or a daily total computed from the very value we predict. Ask of every feature: will I have this at the moment I need the prediction?

title.text:
Keep this checklist: five questions
before you trust a score

objects.text: Was the score measured on held-out data (rows the model never saw)?
Were the imputer and the scaler fitted on the training set only (no preprocessing leakage)?
Is every feature available at the moment you need the prediction, and none built from the target (no target leakage)?
Is the test set (group E6) still sealed, to be opened once after the final choice?
Is the score a cross-validation mean, shown with its standard deviation?

slides.notes:
Here is the checklist I want you to keep. Questions one to four apply in the project too, and all five return in Class 4. One: was the score measured on held-out data, rows the model never saw?

Two: were the imputer and the scaler fitted on the training set only?

Three: is every feature available at the moment you need the prediction, and none built from the target?

Four: is the test set, group E6, still sealed, to be opened once after the final choice?

Five: is the score a cross-validation mean, shown with its standard deviation?

If you can answer yes to all five, you may trust the number a little. If you cannot, find out why before you show it to anyone.

title.text:
The same code can give different numbers, so we fix
the random seed (random_state) and write it down

rows.text: max_depth chosen by the 5 percent rule

objects.text: MAE in kWh/t. Only the seed changed. The chosen max_depth is the same for every seed here.

slides.notes:
Random choices sit inside many tools. A tree breaks ties at random, and shuffled folds mix the rows at random. A random seed, which scikit-learn calls random_state, is a number that makes those choices repeat exactly. With the same data and code, the depth-10 tree scores 1.21, 1.18 or 1.28 kWh/t, depending on the seed.

The last column reruns our tuning rule with each seed. The chosen max_depth is 5 with every seed here: the choice is stable for this data. So a number without its seed is only half a result. We use random_state equal to seventeen everywhere. Why does a colleague need your seed?

title.text: Write down what you ran, so anyone can repeat it

objects.alt: Write down what you ran, so anyone can repeat it

objects.text: Anyone with this record should get your numbers. After cleaning in Class 1, 88 rows remain: 58, 15, 15.

runs.text: The notebook prints the record for you.
Paste it under every result you report.

slides.notes:
Reproducibility means that someone else, or you in six months, can run the same code and get the same numbers. For that you need a short record. Which data file, and how many rows. After cleaning in Class 1, the usable rows are fewer than the rows in the file, and the record says so.

How the rows were split. The random seed. And the versions of Python, NumPy, pandas and scikit-learn, because a new version can change a result slightly. The notebook prints this record in the last step. Paste it under every result you report. It takes ten seconds. Who in your team would need to repeat your numbers?

title.text: Trust comes from four habits

objects.text: The project needs all but cross-validation, which returns in Class 4.

slides.notes:
Let us gather it up in four habits. Score on rows the model never saw. Use cross-validation, so you report a mean with a standard deviation, and GroupKFold when the model will meet new machines. Fit every preprocessing step, the imputer and the scaler, on the training set only.

And keep a record for reproducibility: the random seed, the data file and the versions. With these four habits, a score becomes something you can defend. Before the break, say aloud which habit you are most likely to forget.

title.text: Read the workflow before you write it

runs.text: pipeline = make_pipeline(imputer, tree_model)
group_kfold = GroupKFold(n_splits=4)
cv_scores = -cross_val_score(
pipeline, X_train, y_train,
groups=groups, cv=group_kfold,
scoring=
"neg_mean_absolute_error"
print(cv_scores.mean(), cv_scores.std(ddof=1))

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: make_pipeline chains the imputer and the tree into one model (a Pipeline).
GroupKFold(n_splits=4): each fold holds out one equipment group.
cross_val_score runs the pipeline on every fold: one score per fold.
The scoring gives the MAE with a minus sign; the minus in front turns it back.
std(ddof=1): sample standard deviation (divide by k - 1).

slides.notes:
Before the break, here is the workflow in seven lines. First the Pipeline: the imputer and the tree, chained into one model, so the imputer is fitted inside every fold. Then GroupKFold with four splits, so each fold holds out one equipment group, and we pass the group labels with groups.

Then cross_val_score, which runs that pipeline on every fold and returns one score per fold. The scoring name has the word neg in it, because scikit-learn likes bigger to be better, so errors come back negative. We put a minus in front to get the MAE back. Finally we print the mean and the standard deviation, with ddof equals 1 so it divides by k minus 1. In the lab you run it.
